lessons.unit: Unit 1: Of Mice and Men - context and title
lessons.title: Of Mice and Men: America in the 1930s and the American Dream
objectives: Describe the Great Depression and the lives of migrant workers
Explain the idea of the American Dream
Link context to how a writer's world shapes a text (AO4)

keywords.def: the severe economic collapse of the 1930s, with mass unemployment and poverty
a person who moves from place to place to find work
the belief that anyone can succeed through hard work
the time, place and events that shape a text
a story shorter than a novel but longer than a short story

starter: Bismillah. Define the term ‘context’ in one sentence.
Name one war poem from last half-term's unit and its poet.
What is the difference between evidence and explanation?

teach.heading: America in the 1930s
bullets: Banks and businesses failed; millions lost jobs
Drought turned farmland to dust in the Midwest
teach.note: Say bismillah. Show the 1936 photograph ‘Migrant Mother’ by Dorothea Lange (Library of Congress, public domain). Give pupils 60 seconds to write down three words describing the woman's expression and what she might be thinking. Take responses. Stress that real families suffered, and that Islam teaches compassion for those in need. Explain the Great Depression through human stories, not only statistics.

teach.heading: Who was Steinbeck?
bullets: John Steinbeck: born in Salinas, California, 1902
Worked on farms and ranches as a young man
Published Of Mice and Men in 1937
Wrote about ordinary working people with sympathy
teach.note: Explain that Steinbeck knew ranch life from experience, which is why his setting feels so real. Of Mice and Men is a novella set in the Salinas Valley. Ask: ‘Why does it matter that a writer has experienced what they write about?’ Possible: authenticity, empathy. Context and writer's purpose are part of AO3.

teach.heading: Migrant ranch workers
bullets: Travelled between ranches for short-term jobs
Low wages, shared bunkhouses, little security
Few possessions: often a bindle (a bundle of belongings)
Often lonely; no home, no family nearby
teach.note: Ask: ‘How would your life change if you had no fixed home?’ Point out that many workers, men and women, faced prejudice and had little power. The novella shows men who are vulnerable because of poverty, disability, age, race or gender. Be prepared for sensitive points: the text contains discriminatory language of its time; teach it with care and explain that it reflects prejudice that the novella itself questions.

teach.heading: The American Dream
bullets: Idea: work hard and you can own your own land
In the Depression it was out of reach for many
Steinbeck asks: is the dream achievable?
teach.note: Introduce the dream with the words ‘freedom’, ‘ownership’, ‘security’. Ask: ‘Why was the dream so attractive to men with nothing?’ Ask pupils to define their own dream in one sentence. Link to the Tarbiyyah Compass value of Contentment (qana'ah): the Prophet (peace be upon him) taught that true richness is richness of the soul, not wealth (Bukhari and Muslim). Discuss the contrast: contentment versus the pressure to own more.

practice: Match: (a) Wall Street Crash (b) migrant worker (c) bindle (d) American Dream to: 1) belief in success through hard work; 2) bundle of belongings; 3) 1929 collapse; 4) person who moves for work.
Look at the Migrant Mother photograph. Write three sentences describing what you see, then one sentence inferring what she feels.
How might loneliness be common among migrant workers? Give two reasons.
independent: Write a 100-word descriptive paragraph about the Migrant Mother photograph, using three adjectives and one simile.
Write a paragraph explaining what the American Dream means and why it might feel out of reach during the Depression.
Extension: explain why context helps us understand a writer's choices (AO4).
exit: Define migrant worker in your own words.
Why was the American Dream attractive in the 1930s?
lessons.homework: Research the Great Depression and write five bullet facts with sources. Include one fact about ordinary families.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a one-page context fact sheet with images. EAL: pre-teach ‘migrant’, ‘bindle’, ‘ranch’. Stretch: compare the 1930s Depression with a modern economic crisis.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Of Mice and Men - context and title
lessons.title: The title and a poem: Burns's To a Mouse and plans that go wrong
objectives: Explain the origin and meaning of the title
Annotate a short extract of a poem for language and meaning
Predict themes of the novella using the title and context

keywords.def: a reference to another text, person or event
a central idea in a text
hints about what will happen later
a regional way of speaking, with its own words and grammar
a reasoned guess about what will happen

starter: Name two features of the 1930s migrant worker's life.
What does ‘American Dream’ mean?
Define theme.

teach.heading: Robert Burns, 1785
bullets: He accidentally destroyed a mouse's nest with his plough
Steinbeck took his title from the poem
teach.note: Say bismillah. Explain that the poem is written in Scots dialect. Burns speaks to a mouse whose home he has ruined while ploughing. Ask: ‘How would a mouse feel to lose its home in winter?’ Read the famous lines aloud: ‘The best-laid schemes o' Mice an' Men / Gang aft agley’. Do not expect pupils to know Scots words; give a glossary.

teach.heading: What do the lines mean?
bullets: Mice and men are alike: both vulnerable
teach.note: Paraphrase: the best-made plans of mice and people often go wrong. Ask: ‘Have you ever planned something carefully that went wrong?’ Share examples. Link to Islamic belief in tawakkul and qadr: we make a plan and trust in Allah, knowing the outcome is in His hands. Keep this respectful and tied to the text: the novella is about human plans and fragility, not a theological argument.

teach.heading: Predicting themes
teach.note: Show the title and cover images from several editions. Ask pupils to predict who ‘mice’ and ‘men’ might refer to. Possible answers: the weak and vulnerable, the poor, ordinary workers. Record predictions on a shared board. We will return to them after Chapter 1 and Chapter 2.

teach.heading: Foreshadowing and the title
bullets: A title can hint at the ending
The mouse's ruined home foreshadows trouble
Readers sense that dreams may be at risk
Think about why a writer gives clues early
teach.note: Define foreshadowing and ask pupils to recall one example from a story they know. Explain that Steinbeck's title signals that the characters' dreams may not survive. Ask: ‘Does knowing it might end badly make you read differently?’ Possible: more anxious, more attentive to details.

practice: Rewrite in modern English: ‘The best-laid schemes o' Mice an' Men / Gang aft agley.’
Give one example from your own life or the news where a careful plan went wrong.
Which theme do you think the title most strongly suggests? Explain in two sentences.
independent: Write a paragraph (6-8 sentences): What do you think the novella will be about, based on its title and the context? Use the words ‘theme’, ‘foreshadow’ and ‘vulnerable’.
Write four lines of your own poem addressed to a small creature whose home has been disturbed, using direct address.
Extension: write two sentences comparing the fate of the mouse to the lives of migrant workers.
exit: Explain in your own words what the title suggests.
Define foreshadowing and give a simple example.
lessons.homework: Write a short response: Why might a writer choose a title that comes from another text? Include the word ‘allusion’.
lessons.send: SEND: give a paraphrase sheet for the poem lines. EAL: glossary for ‘plough’, ‘scheme’, ‘vulnerable’. Stretch: look up one more stanza of the Burns poem and explain how the speaker feels.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Of Mice and Men - Chapter 1
lessons.title: Chapter 1 setting: how Steinbeck creates an atmosphere
objectives: Analyse how Steinbeck uses description to present the setting
Link word choices to atmosphere and symbolism
Apply the same approach to an unseen description (AQA Language-style)

keywords.def: where and when a story takes place
the mood or feeling created in a text
when nature reflects human feelings
words appealing to the five senses
using an object or place to stand for an idea

starter: Define foreshadowing.
What are two themes you predicted last lesson?
Give one example of a simile.

teach.heading: The opening paragraph
bullets: ‘The Salinas River… runs deep and green’
Precise place: real geography near Soledad
teach.note: Say bismillah. Read the opening paragraph aloud from the class copy and ask pupils to close their eyes and visualise it. Take three words they would use to describe the mood: peaceful, warm, safe. Misconception: that setting is only background. It sets mood, hints at themes, and may symbolise ideas.

teach.heading: Word choices
bullets: ‘Deep and green’: colours of life and calm
teach.note: Ask pupils to find verbs and adjectives that create a peaceful atmosphere. Model a PEE answer: ‘Steinbeck describes the river as ‘deep and green’, which suggests a calm, safe place, perhaps a refuge from the harshness of working life.’ Notice that the list of details feels unhurried.

teach.heading: Something beneath the calm
bullets: Footprints and tracks near the pool
Hints that this is a place to hide
teach.note: Look at the details of animal and human tracks near the water. Explain that the setting is peaceful but not empty: others have passed here. Ask: ‘What might the writer suggest about the characters who stop here?’ Introduce the idea that a place can offer both beauty and a sense of unease. Use your class text for exact references.

teach.heading: Link to Language Paper 1
bullets: AQA Q2: how does the writer use language?
Name the technique and explain the effect
Think about mood, not just meaning
teach.note: Explain that setting description is a regular feature of AQA Language Paper 1 Section A. The same skills apply: select short evidence, comment on language, link to atmosphere. Show the structure: Point (what mood), Evidence (short quote), Explain (what the word suggests), Develop (alternative reading). Ask pupils how they will approach an unseen description using this approach.

practice: Find three words or phrases from the opening paragraph that create a peaceful mood. Explain one in full.

Read this teacher-written description: ‘The pond lay still under a low sun. Reeds whispered at the edge, and a heron stood like a grey statue, waiting. The water was the colour of old pewter.’ What atmosphere does it create? Use two quotes.
Why might Steinbeck begin the novella with a beautiful, peaceful place?
independent: Write a paragraph (7-8 sentences): How does Steinbeck present the setting in the opening of Chapter 1? Include two short quotations and use the words ‘atmosphere’ and ‘suggests’.
Write a short description (6-8 sentences) of a peaceful place near water, using three senses and a simile.
Extension: add a sentence hinting at danger to create foreshadowing.
exit: Write a PEE sentence about the word ‘green’ in the opening.
Why is setting more than a backdrop?
lessons.homework: Complete the paragraph on Steinbeck's setting using the feedback in class. Underline the technique and the effect.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a highlighted extract and sentence starters. EAL: picture glossary for river, hillside, willows. Stretch: compare to the opening of another novel or text you have read.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Of Mice and Men - Chapter 1
lessons.title: Chapter 1: meeting George and Lennie
objectives: Compare how George and Lennie are presented in description and dialogue
Select and analyse short quotations about each man
Explain what their contrast suggests about their relationship

keywords.def: a main character in a story
the ways a writer builds a character, through description, speech and actions
a strong difference between two things
words spoken by characters
a comparison using like or as

starter: What mood does the opening setting create?
Give one technique Steinbeck uses to build atmosphere.
Define dialogue.

teach.heading: George: small and sharp
bullets: ‘small and quick, dark of face, with restless eyes and sharp, strong features’
Describes himself as responsible for Lennie
Speaks with irritation but also care
teach.note: Say bismillah. Read the description of George and ask pupils to find adjectives. Ask: ‘What does ‘restless eyes’ tell us?’ Possible: always watchful, anxious, alert for danger. Misconception: George is simply mean to Lennie. Show later that his scolding hides loyalty and fear for Lennie.

teach.heading: Lennie: large and bear-like
bullets: ‘the way a bear drags his paws’
teach.note: Read the description of Lennie. Notice the simile comparing him to a bear: strong, powerful, but also clumsy and gentle. Ask: ‘What is the effect of comparing a man to an animal?’ Possible: emphasises his size and innocence, but also risks making him seem less than human, a sign of how society views him. Note Lennie imitates George's actions, which shows dependence.

teach.heading: Contrast and balance
bullets: Small, quick George and large, slow Lennie
teach.note: Use a Venn diagram: George / both / Lennie. Pupils add at least three points to each area. Ask: ‘What do they have in common?’ Possible: dream, loyalty, fear of being alone. Explain how contrast helps readers to understand both characters.

teach.heading: Dialogue and relationship
bullets: Lennie asks to hear the story of the dream
Their bond is deeper than boss and worker
teach.note: Read a short exchange from the class text. Ask: ‘Who has the power, and does it feel that way?’ Pupils should notice that George can leave but stays. Link to Islamic values: the Prophet (peace be upon him) said that none of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself (Bukhari and Muslim). Discuss how George shows care towards a vulnerable person.

practice: Write one quotation about George and one about Lennie. For each, state the technique and effect.
Complete the sentence: ‘The simile ‘the way a bear drags his paws’ suggests Lennie is…’
In pairs: what does George gain from having Lennie, and what does he lose?
independent: Write a paragraph (7-8 sentences): How does Steinbeck present the differences between George and Lennie in Chapter 1? Use two quotations, one about each man.
Add a sentence beginning ‘However, they are similar because…’
Extension: write two sentences exploring how the ‘bear’ simile could be read in more than one way.
exit: Give one way George cares for Lennie in Chapter 1.
lessons.homework: Write a diary entry as Lennie describing his journey with George, using language that reflects his character.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a character table with sentence starters. EAL: pre-teach ‘restless’, ‘shapeless’, ‘sloping’. Stretch: analyse how Steinbeck uses George's speech to show tension between irritation and care.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Of Mice and Men - Chapter 1
lessons.title: Chapter 1: friendship, loneliness and the dream
objectives: Explain how Steinbeck presents friendship and loneliness
Analyse the dream of the farm and its significance
Identify foreshadowing in Chapter 1

keywords.def: the sadness of being without company or friends
a bond of trust and care between people
a hope for a better future
a repeated image or idea in a text
hints about what will happen later

starter: What does George's description suggest about him?
Write one sentence comparing George and Lennie.
Define motif.

teach.heading: Loneliness on the ranch
bullets: ‘Guys like us, that work on ranches, are the loneliest guys in the world.’
Workers have no family or home
teach.note: Say bismillah. Read George's speech about the loneliness of ranch workers from the class text. Ask: ‘Why does George say this?’ Possible: to explain why friendship is precious. Misconception: the men are lonely because they choose to be. Their circumstances, poverty and constant moving, make friendships hard. Link to Islamic teaching about brotherhood and community, and the Qur'an's teaching that Allah loves those who do good (2:195).

teach.heading: ‘We got a future’
bullets: ‘Somebody to talk to that gives a damn about us’
They are different from other men
teach.note: Read the exchange aloud with two pupils as George and Lennie. Ask what makes their relationship special. Note the repetition of ‘we got’, which makes the friendship feel solid, and ‘gives a damn’, which shows the emotional need. Ask: ‘Is it healthy for Lennie to rely so much on George?’ Discuss both sides.

teach.heading: The dream farm
bullets: George tells the story like a bedtime ritual
Lennie asks to hear it again
teach.note: Explain that the dream is repeated like a story told to a child, a ritual that soothes. Rabbits appeal to Lennie because he loves soft things. Ask: ‘What does this ritual show about their friendship and hopes?’ Link to context: the American Dream. Discuss how the dream gives the men dignity.

teach.heading: Hints of trouble
bullets: The dead mouse in Lennie's pocket
Setting reminds us this refuge is temporary
teach.note: Explain Lennie's habit of petting small things too hard. Ask: ‘What does the dead mouse suggest about what could happen later?’ Possible: Lennie does not know his own strength. This is foreshadowing. Be careful to discuss without spoilers if some pupils have not finished reading. Remind pupils that you will analyse the consequences in later lessons.

practice: Find two quotations that show the importance of friendship. Explain one.
What do the words ‘we got’ and ‘gives a damn’ suggest about George's feelings?
Give two pieces of evidence of foreshadowing in Chapter 1.
independent: Write a paragraph (7-8 sentences): How does Steinbeck present loneliness and friendship in Chapter 1? Use two quotations and refer to context.
Create a short 5-line poem or ‘dream list’ for George and Lennie's farm, using concrete nouns and adjectives.
Extension: explain in two sentences how the dream could be both hopeful and dangerous.
exit: Define motif and give one possible motif in Chapter 1.
Why is George's friendship with Lennie unusual among ranch workers?
lessons.homework: Write 6-8 sentences: Why do you think Steinbeck repeats the dream story in Chapter 1?
lessons.send: SEND: provide quotation cards and a sentence frame. EAL: glossary for ‘loneliest’, ‘ritual’, ‘gives a damn’. Stretch: compare the role of friendship here with another text you have studied.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Of Mice and Men - Chapter 2 and writing the response
lessons.title: Chapter 2: the ranch, power and suspicion
objectives: Explain how the bunkhouse setting shows the lives of ranch workers
Analyse how Steinbeck presents power and hierarchy
Select evidence about Candy, the Boss and Curley

keywords.def: a system of ranks with some people having more power than others
a building where workers sleep
a feeling that someone cannot be trusted
easily harmed or in need of protection
a feeling of anxiety or conflict

starter: What does the simile ‘the way a bear drags his paws’ suggest?
Give one quotation about friendship in Chapter 1.
Define foreshadowing.

teach.heading: The bunkhouse
bullets: Rows of beds and few belongings
Setting shows how little workers own
teach.note: Say bismillah. Read the description of the bunkhouse from the class copy. Ask pupils to list what is there and what is missing. Ask: ‘What does this tell you about the men's lives?’ Compare with the peaceful setting in Chapter 1. Possible contrast: nature as refuge versus work as hardship. Note that setting changes from nature to human-made.

teach.heading: Who has power?
bullets: Candy: old and fears losing his place
teach.note: Use a pyramid diagram on a shared whiteboard to rank the characters by power. Ask: ‘Who is vulnerable and why?’ Possible: Candy because of age and disability; Lennie because of mind; Crooks later because of race. Explain the idea of a hierarchy and note how fear of losing work keeps workers quiet. Introduce Curley as small, aggressive, and likely to pick fights with bigger men. Do not reveal later plot developments.

teach.heading: Suspicion and insecurity
bullets: The Boss questions why George and Lennie travel together
George speaks for Lennie to protect him
teach.note: Link to Chapter 1: George and Lennie's friendship is unusual. The Boss assumes George must be taking advantage of Lennie. Ask: ‘Why would he think this?’ Possible: workers are used to selfishness and exploitation. Note how George lies for Lennie to protect him, which is a moral grey area. Discuss in the light of truthfulness: when is protecting someone justified, and what are the risks?

teach.heading: Building tension
bullets: Curley arrives looking for a fight
teach.note: Explain that Steinbeck builds tension through dialogue, warnings and short exchanges. Ask: ‘Which character do you feel most nervous about?’ Pupils should justify with evidence. Remind pupils to quote briefly and avoid retelling. Handle language carefully: if the class edition contains offensive racial language, explain its historical context and avoid reading it aloud unnecessarily.

practice: Make a power ranking of the Boss, Curley, Candy, George and Lennie, from most to least power. Justify your top and bottom choices.
Find two details of the bunkhouse. What does each suggest about the workers' lives?
Why might George speak for Lennie when the Boss asks questions?
independent: Write a paragraph (7-8 sentences): How does Steinbeck present power and fear on the ranch in Chapter 2? Use two short quotations and the word ‘hierarchy’.
Write four sentences predicting how Curley will affect George and Lennie. Use evidence.
Extension: explain how the ranch contrasts with the setting in Chapter 1.
exit: Define hierarchy and give an example from the novel.
Which character do you think is most vulnerable on the ranch? Why?
lessons.homework: Write a diary entry as Candy on the day George and Lennie arrive, showing his fears and hopes.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a character-power grid and quotation list. EAL: use images for bunkhouse and ranch tools. Stretch: compare the ranch hierarchy with a workplace or school hierarchy today.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Of Mice and Men - Chapter 2 and writing the response
lessons.title: Chapter 2: Curley's wife - how is she introduced?
objectives: Analyse how Steinbeck introduces Curley's wife
Explain how she is seen by the men and what this reveals
Link to the position of women in 1930s America (AO4)

keywords.def: a fixed, oversimplified idea about a type of person
being separated from others
a society in which men hold most power
to treat a person as a thing rather than a human being
a particular way of seeing something

starter: Define hierarchy.
Give one example of tension in Chapter 2.
Why is Candy vulnerable?

teach.heading: She has no name
bullets: Defined by her husband, not herself
The reader should notice this absence
teach.note: Say bismillah. Ask pupils what it says about a character if she is never given a name. Possible: she is seen as property, not a person. Teach: in 1930s America women had limited independence and opportunity, especially on remote ranches. Be thoughtful: we are analysing a writer's presentation, not endorsing it.

teach.heading: First appearance
bullets: She stands in the doorway, blocking the light
Dressed to be noticed; looking for Curley
George warns Lennie to stay away
teach.note: Read her entrance from the class text. Ask: ‘Why does Steinbeck place her in the doorway?’ Possible: she is both an intruder and an outsider; the light is blocked, hinting at threat or restriction. Pupils should find short quotations about her appearance, using the class edition. Misconception: that she is only a villain. Steinbeck also shows her loneliness.

teach.heading: How the men see her
bullets: Candy and others call her trouble
teach.note: Discuss stereotypes: the men assume she is flirtatious and a threat. Ask: ‘Do we hear her side yet?’ Possible: only partly, and she says she is lonely. The reader must weigh the men's view against her few words. Encourage pupils to hold a balanced view and recognise that characters can be judged unfairly. In Islam, we are taught to avoid suspicion and assumptions about others; discuss how that could apply to reading characters.

teach.heading: Loneliness and isolation
bullets: She has no friends on the ranch
teach.note: Link to Chapter 1's loneliness theme. Ask: ‘How is her loneliness different from George and Lennie's?’ Possible: they have each other; she has no one. Show how Steinbeck builds sympathy by hints rather than statements. Prepare for the later chapters by noting the idea of dreams: even she has hopes. Do not give plot spoilers.

practice: Find two details about Curley's wife's first appearance from the class text and explain what each suggests.
Why might Steinbeck leave her unnamed? Write two reasons.
Complete: ‘The men see Curley's wife as…, but the reader may see her as…’
independent: Write a paragraph (7-8 sentences): How does Steinbeck introduce Curley's wife in Chapter 2? Use two short quotations and refer to the position of women in the 1930s.
Write a short monologue (5-6 sentences) from Curley's wife on the first day George and Lennie arrive. Show her loneliness.
Extension: explain how perspective changes how we judge her.
exit: Define stereotype and give an example from the text.
Why might readers feel sympathy for Curley's wife?
lessons.homework: Rewrite your paragraph, adding a sentence of context (AO4) and checking that every quotation is short and accurate.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a quotation bank and sentence stems. EAL: glossary for ‘intruder’, ‘isolation’, ‘assumption’. Stretch: explore how a modern text presents a lonely character differently.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Of Mice and Men - Chapter 2 and writing the response
lessons.title: Writing the response: a whole-text essay (bridge to International GCSE modern prose)
objectives: Plan and write an exam-style response on the whole text
Embed short quotations and weave in context
Use the Pearson Edexcel International GCSE English Literature assessment objectives to self-assess

keywords.def: show close knowledge of the text, with a critical style and personal engagement
analyse the writer's language, form and structure
explore links and connections between texts
show understanding of the context the text was written in
a clear overall argument or idea in an essay

starter: Write a PEE sentence about Curley's wife.
Define stereotype.
Name one context (AO4) point from this unit.

teach.heading: Reading the question
bullets: Question: How does Steinbeck present George and Lennie's friendship?
Plan: 3 ideas, each with a short quotation
teach.note: Say bismillah. Link to the Year 10 course: Of Mice and Men is one of the modern prose set texts for Pearson Edexcel International GCSE English Literature (Component 1 Section C). That exam is closed book and marks AO1 and AO4 equally, so pupils need to know the text well and use context. Show a plain question and ask pupils to circle the command words. Misconception: the question is ‘What happens?’. It asks ‘how’, which means methods.

teach.heading: Planning three ideas
bullets: Idea 2: they care for each other
teach.note: Model a plan with arrows: contrast (small/large, brain/strength), care (George looks after Lennie; ‘I got you to look after me’), dream (‘We got a future’). Pupils copy the plan format and fill it in. Check quotations are short and accurate.

teach.heading: Writing a strong paragraph
bullets: Embed a short quotation in your sentence
Zoom in on a word or technique
Add context (AO4) and link to the question
teach.note: Show an example: ‘Steinbeck presents the friendship as unusual and precious. George's statement ‘We got a future’ shows that the men's bond gives them hope, and the repetition of ‘we’ suggests unity. In a world where ranch workers were often alone, this makes their friendship stand out.’ Ask pupils to find the quotation, the technique, the context and the link.

teach.heading: Self-assessment with AOs
bullets: AO1: clear ideas, close knowledge, quotations
teach.note: Give pupils a checklist with the AOs. AO3 (links between texts) is for comparing poems, so it is not on this checklist. They tick what they have and underline what is missing. Emphasise that top marks require developed ideas, not extra length. Link to the Tarbiyyah Compass value of Excellence: doing our best and learning from feedback. Offer a short dua for ease and success in learning before the writing task.

practice: Turn this weak sentence into a strong one: ‘George is nice to Lennie and it shows they are friends.’
Underline the AO2 technique in: ‘The simile ‘the way a bear drags his paws’ suggests Lennie is strong yet gentle.’
Write one sentence of context (AO4) you could add to a paragraph about friendship.
independent: Write a response of 2-3 paragraphs: How does Steinbeck present the friendship between George and Lennie in Chapter 1? Use at least three short quotations.
Self-assess with the AO checklist. Highlight one improvement you will make.
Extension: write a concluding paragraph that comments on how Chapter 2 develops the idea of loneliness.
exit: Which AO do you find hardest and why?
Write one sentence that embeds a quotation smoothly.
lessons.homework: Redraft your response using your self-assessment and teacher feedback. Aim for 250-300 words.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a paragraph frame and quotation bank. EAL: model sentence starters and glossary. Stretch: add a counter-argument paragraph considering whether George is also dependent on Lennie.

lessons.unit: Autumn 1: The Woman in Black (Susan Hill): fear and the supernatural
lessons.title: Bridge: The Woman in Black, Gothic setting and isolation
lessons.bigQuestion: How does Hill make a place feel dangerous?
objectives: To understand how Susan Hill uses an isolated setting to create psychological fear
successCriteria: All: name three features of Eel Marsh House and its setting
Most: explain how isolation creates fear
Some: write a thesis sentence about Hill's use of setting
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: grief, loss and how people cope

islamicLink.text: Islam teaches belief in the unseen (al-ghayb, الغَيْب), including the jinn, but not that the dead return as ghosts: the souls of the dead are in the barzakh (بَرْزَخ) until the Day of Judgement. We study the ghost story as literature about grief and fear.

keywords.def: being cut off from others
fear that grows in the mind
weather or setting reflecting feelings
the central argument of an essay

hook.text: Is a place frightening in itself, or only because of what we imagine might happen there?

pictures.alt: A tidal causeway across a marsh
Sea fog over a salt marsh
An isolated house on flat marshland
